speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) :

subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGMENT OF GIFT OF PORTRAITS TO BE PLACED IN PARLIAMENT BUILDINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I beg to move, seconded by the right hon. leader of the opposition, the following motion:
That this house deeply appreciates the generous gift made by E. S. Makower, Esquire, of London, England, of a complete collection of portraits of British prime ministers, from the Right Honourable Sir Robert Walpole to the Right Honourable Ramsay MacDonald, which have been placed in the parliament building of Canada; and that the warm thanks of the House of Commons of Canada be conveyed by Mr. Speaker to Mr. Makower.
I dare say that my right hon. friend may think that this is another illustration of the old saying, that one sows and another reaps. The fact is that the arrangements in connection with the gift of these valuable portraits to the Canadian people was arranged by my predecessor in office, who was communicated with, I understand, through the then Prime 22110-282
Minister. It was my privilege and pleasure to receive from Mr. Makower these portraits framed as they now hang upon the walls of the gallery leading to the restaurant. There I trust they will always serve as a reminder to us of the splendour of the achievements of the great and distinguished men who have occupied the position of Prime Minister of Great Britain. In recording our sense of appreciation of this gift, I am sure the resolution conveys the sentiments of every member of this house. It is an additional pleasure to associate my right hon. friend with me in the motion as its seconder.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: ACKNOWLEDGMENT OF GIFT OF PORTRAITS TO BE PLACED IN PARLIAMENT BUILDINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I am indeed happy to have the opportunity or joining with my right hon. friend in approval of the motion which has just been placed in your hands. As my right honourable friend said, it is a case where one sows and another reaps. The sowing has been done by Mr. Makower, and we in Canada, and of this parliament irrespective of the parties to * which we belong, have been reaping the benefits of his generosity. As the Prime Minister has just said, during the time the late Liberal administration was in office I received a communication from the then Prime Minister of Great Britain asking if it would be agreeable with a view to the portraits being placed in our parliament buildings to accept from Mr. Makower on behalf of the government of Canada this splendid collection of portraits of the Prime Ministers of Great Britain from the days of Walpole down to the present time. I expressed to the Prime Minister of Great Britain our warm appreciation of the contemplated gift, and subsequently sent as well a personal word of thanks to Mr. Makower. The gift itself of the collection of portraits was not received until after my right hon. friend came into office, and it is a happy circumstance, that as a consequence each of us has now the pleasure of joining in this acknowledgment, which I am sure will be made wholeheartedly on the part of all hon. members of this House of Commons.
May I say that I understand Mr. Makower's generosity has extended to the making of similar gifts to the British House of Commons and to the parliaments of the other self-governing dominions. It is a noteworthy example of great generosity and public spirit, and I feel that too warm a word of appreciation cannot be expressed for what this parliament has received.
Motion agreed to.

I desire to direct the attention of the Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan) to a press item appearing in this morning's Ottawa Citizen, on which I desire to base a question:
For the first time since civic holiday was inaugurated 21 years ago, the union men at the government printing bureau will not get the day off. speakeroldname: Hon. C. H. CAHAN (Secretary of State):
speechtext:
As to whether the men employed in the printing bureau on prevailing rates are or are not union men, I have no knowledge. Representations have been made to me from time to time that they are largely union men, but I have not yet been able to ascertain the facts. With regard to their holidays, I may say that the men who are at work on prevailing rates are entitled to the highest rates which prevail in the printing trades in Toronto and Montreal, and are paid accordingly. In Toronto and Montreal the men who are paid these rates are entitled only to the statutory holidays. Therefore I see no reason why men who are employed on prevailing rates and who are receiving the highest wages, men who are not in the civil service as such, should receive holidays at the expense of the treasury of Canada. The responsibility is solely mine, but I gave instructions to the King's Printer that hereafter, until he was advised otherwise, printers on prevailing rates who are not members of the civil service should receive no holidays on pay which are not holidays in the printing trades of Toronto and Montreal. I may say that the printing bureau last year ran behind $70,000, and that was due largely to the fact that we were allowing printers on prevailing rates to have holiday after holiday which were not recognized under the statute. Each holiday of that character costs this treasury, in cash, $4,500 or thereabouts. I gave instructions that any printers employed at prevailing rates who wished to celebrate on Monday would have ample opportunity to do so. They were

speechtext:
I cannot regret too deeply that my right hon. friend has not seen his way, I shall not say, to accept the suggestions of the opposition, but to act in accordance with what is everywhere recognized as a fundamental principle, namely the control of the House of Commons over expenditures. I regret that above all because of what it means in the way of violation of the constitution. His refusal constitutes a complete, may I say, submarining of the right and the duty of the commons to control taxation, especially where taxation on so very large a scale will be necessitated in order to meet a situation such as the Prime Minister contemplates by this measure. Let me say to my right hon. friend that I believe I appreciate the reasons why he takes the position he does at the moment. I believe him to be sincere in the statement he has given us of those reasons; but I believe he would hardly have given them were it not for the fact that, having so completely in mind the seriousness of the position with which we are faced in the country owing to the extent of unemployment and the possibility of that situation becoming still more serious, he has lost the larger vision of a matter which is more important than all else, namely, the necessity of keeping parliament supreme in dealing with all questions of great national concern. My right hon. friend has spoken as though it were the duty of the executive regardless of parliament altogether tp deal with the problems that may arise within the next few months. In that attitude I think he is quite mistaken. If a grave situation should arise, it would be his duty to have parliament summoned to cope with it. That is the all-important point which my right hon. friend seems to lose sight of altogether.
The House of Commons is the committee of the nation appointed by the people at large above all else to control appropria-
4450	COMMONS

tions of public money which may be necessary to deal with all situations as they may arise. The importance of summoning the commons at a moment to enact the measures necessary to deal with any great question cannot be exaggerated. The security of the nation, peace, order, good government-all of these matters have their foundation in the fact that under our system of responsible government, under our British constitution, the people's representatives may be brought- together at any moment to cope with any situation which affects their rights and well being. My right hon. friend appeared to recognize that last year when conditions were not at all comparable with what they are to-day. In September of last year he summoned a special session of 'parliament on account of the unemployment situation. Why should he not summon a special session of parliament this September to deal with unemployment if the situation' at that time demands it. He will not have any Imperial conference to attend this year; he will have the intervening month or two to rest up after the present session. Otherwise, why can he not bring parliament into regular session in the month of November, if need be, rather than attempt, himself with the aid only of his colleagues, to deal with a great national emergency. The stronger the reasons presented by my right hon. friend why unlimited powers should be given his executive, the stronger, in my mind, becomes the necessity of his remembering the obligation which rests at all times upon the government to bring together collectively the people's representatives to cope with any great national question, and not to leave a national emergency to be dealt with by any committee of parliament, albeit the committee which constitutes the cabinet.
I am just afraid the course my right hon. friend has taken in this matter may help to aggravate the condition with which he is faced. It creates another situation more serious, it seems to me, than anything we can contemplate at the moment. No one can tell what condition may arise. My right hon. friend, in asking for these additional powers in connection with peace, order and good government raises at once an alarm in the mind of the country that he is contemplating something dangerous. The whole seriousness of that situation will be increased if the people get into their heads the idea that no matter what happens parliament is not to be summoned until on in the spring of next year. I hope my right hon. friend will, before parliament prorogues, make it quite clear that
IMr. Mackenzie King.]
if there does arise in Canada a situation-and let us pray it will not arise-of a very serious character, he will immediately summon the people's representatives. In that way; and that way alone, will we escape the effects of what comes inevitably from autocratic and coercive action. I am genuinely alarmed as to the possible effect of some of the provisions of this measure through what they may occasion in the way of riots and violence in different parts of the country. Powers will be given to officers or individuals who have had little or no experience with the enforcement of law. With this great authority behind them which at the moment, the government of the day is taking from parliament, they will feel free to act to the limit; that will believe that the executive has absolute authority in regard to all moneys required and in regard to the force that may be needed. This thing of itself may create a condition of unrest, if not of strife, such perhaps as we have not seen in this country at any time. I do not believe that one can stress that possibility too strongly, and it is because I am hoping and praying that nothing of the kind may occur, and am seeking to have this parliament preserved in its rights to deal with any situation of a serious kind, that I make this strong appeal to my right hon. friend. Parliament should not part with its control over the executive. That is what it is being asked by this bill to do.
Let me repeat, there is a consideration above all other considerations not only with respect to peace, order and good government, but with respect to all that pertains to our constitution and to the making of laws, and that is that at all times parliament may be summoned at a moment's notice and that when parliament is summoned the people's representatives in parliament shall have complete control over the executive and its acts, particularly as regards those measures which involve increased taxation.
I am not going to try to elaborate that idea by words of my own, but in order to surround the whole matter with the solemnity which I think is its due I wish to quote a paragraph or two from a treatise which is recognized throughout the British Empire as the standard work on parliamentary grants. I have in my hand the volume, which is entitled The Principles and Practice of the System of Control over Parliamentary Grants, by Colonel A. I. V. sDurell, C.B. May I read two or three significant paragraphs and ask hon. members, as the representatives of the people, elected to maintain their freedom and their rights, and above all to sustain and maintain the tradi-

Farm and Unemployment Relief
tions of parliament and responsible government, to weigh in their minds the significance of these few words. On page 2 the writer says:
The bedrock on which the English system is built is the principle of the maintenance by parliament of control over the grants which it makes.
This bedrock on which the English system is built is being shattered by the act of the administration in refusing to allow this House of Commons to fix any amount in connection with the purpose of this particular bill.
Now I come to the section of this work which deals with the constitutional aspect of these grants. On page 3 I find the following:
It is one of the old standing principles of our constitution that the House of Commons should control the finances of the country. That is the right, privilege and duty of the house. It has been achieved by means of struggles lasting through centuries, beginning from the fourteenth century down to the seventeenth century, when it was fully confirmed, and since then it has never been practically disputed. "Ut quod omnes tangit, ab omnibus approbetur." The quotation by Edward I of this legal maxim transmitted it into a great and constitutional principle. In other words, the cardinal principle on which the whole of our financial system is based is that of parliamentary control, and by this is understood not the control of parliament in its constitutional sense as composed of Sovereign, Lords and Commons, but control by the Commons alone.
My right hon. friend has a great regard for one other authority whom he has quoted' many times in this House of Commons, and that is Redlieh, on the House of Commons. Here is a quotation on the very page from which I am reading, from Redlieh, chapter iii, page 114:
Upon this fundamental principle, laid down at the very outset of English parliamentary history and secured by three hundred years of mingled conflict with the crown and peaceful growth, is grounded the whole law' of finance and, consequently, the wdiole British constitution.
Surely my right hon. friend in the pressure of a very strenuous session, and dealing with an extraordinarily difficult -situation must have had his mind so preoccupied with the immediate thing that he has lost sight altogether of the larger principles which he above all others should maintain, and, may I add, which I believe in his heart of hearts he as much as any other is anxious to see maintained. I believe my right hon. friend has a real reverence for parliament; I think he has an equal reverence for the institutions of parliament, and I find myself at a loss to understand how, excepting under the pressure of tremendous strain through a long session, he could have been
tempted to take what seems to be the easy path and the short path in dealing with the problem that he is dealing with here in the manner in which he is dealing with it. May I go just a step further? A quotation from Todd's Parliamentary Government is given on this same page from which I have been quoting:
The most ancient, as well as the most valued, prerogative of the House of Commons is the right of supreme control over taxation, to which the right to control issues is a natural corollary.
I say, Mr. Speaker, that those words ought to be emblazoned on the walls of this chamber to be constantly before the mind of every hon. member who sits in this house.

I do not intend to discus3 the principle of the bill; I pronounced myself in that regard when the resolution was before the house. I wish, however, to direct the attention of the Prime Minister to a situation that has developed, at least in the province of New Brunswick. This act, section 1 declares, may be cited as the Unemployment and Farm Relief Act, 1931. 1 do not see in any section of the bill any specific reference to what section of the country the relief will

apply. I suppose the government would be prepared to consider requests for relief from farmers or settlers in any section of Canada, provided the request was not exceptional in character. In New Brunswick a great many people settle on what are known as green farms. They get the right to do so from the local government under the colonization statute of the province. They are obliged to clear ten acres of land, and to build a house, whether it be a log house or not, twenty feet by fourteen, together with a barn. They clear the land and live on it for three years and after that they have title. This local colonization has been carried on to quite an extent in northern New Brunswick. In the last three or four years a number of people have taken up these green farms and have hewn homes for themselves out of the forest. Under the act they are allowed to absent themselves from their farms during a period of four months. That period takes in the summer season. After they have put in what crop they can, they are allowed to go and earn a living elsewhere, the land not having yet reached that state of cultivation which will enable them to live entirely from the crops grown on it. In the past they have been able to sell pulpwood from the first ten acres, and when these ten acres are cleared and put under cultivation they are permitted to take up a further ten acres adjacent. In this way they have been able to eke out a living and bring up their little families, clearing the land and selling the timber for pulp-wood. In winter, if they are not engaged getting out pulpwood, they have an opportunity-at least they had in the past-of going to the lumber camps in large numbers. Within the last three or four years, however, winter operations in the lumber camps, as everyone . knows, owing to economic conditions, have not provided much employment, and in some parts of New Brunswick labour has dwindled to practically nothing. Last winter in northern New Brunswick there was little lumbering carried on. The price of pulpwood in the local market has fallen to practically nothing. In fact, there is little demand for it at the present time except in one section in northern New Brunswick. Now, these people find themselves in this position. While there is not a crop failure, as in the west, they have not in the last four or five years had the means of earning a living while at the same time building up homes for themselves in the forest. I know certain sections of northern New Brunswick where the people are in a desperate condition to-day, and I would ask the Prime Minister whether, in the event of a request

Mr. Chairman, the
Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) must be thanked for the justification he has given for

the criticisms made both on the resolution and the second reading of this bill. I expected nothing else from the right hon. gentleman, knowing his principles and his traditions. I think every hon. member expected it, and I trust the youthful member of the government, the Solicitor General (Mr. Dupre), will be able to profit therefrom. I was painfully surprised at the remarks of the Solicitor General. I have known him to be a young man of principle, and I hope his twelve months in office have not yet made him cynical with regard to the maintenance of the basic principles of government.
I will not say anything further with regard to the fixing of an amount. The amendment now before the committee expresses the views which I stated when the resolution was introduced. In some respects, I agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. AVoodsworth), while in other respects I disagree. I also both agree and disagree with the hon. member for Toronto Northwest (Mr. MacNicol) who spoke last night. I believe that there is possibility of danger, especially in the large centres, and I hold that it is one of the primary duties of the government to make preparations to guard against such dangers. The government has the duty and the responsibility of looking after the welfare of all classes of the community in all parts of the country. The maintenance of peace is one of the essentials of the liberty of the subject. Poor people could not be relieved if peace were not maintained. However, on the other hand, I agree with the hon. member from Toronto West Centre (Mr. Factor), and with my hon. friend in this corner of the chamber (Mr. Woods-worth) that the form in which this legislation is presented is not the form which should have been adopted by the government in order, first, to accomplish its bounden duty to keep peace and order and, second, to counteract the attempt which will be made by those wanting to create disorder. No doubt the revolutionaries, call them bolsheviks or communists, are very few in number; I do not think they are dangerous in or by themselves and I think it was a mistake upon the part of the hon. member for Toronto Northwest (Mr. MacNicol) to have given the impression that the communists in Toronto are as numerous or as active as they appear to be from the printed sheets he has read. The danger that I see is this, that you have a large number of good people, usually law-abiding, who, in the state of suffering and anguish in which they find themselves,

may lend their ears to the enterprises and propaganda of individuals who will lead them into crime, although in themselves they are no more criminals than any of us here, and perhaps less than some of us. That is what I am afraid of. It seems to me in order to have the moral force of public opinion, especially among those people for whom this legislation is meant, I mean the sufferers, the government should have made it clear they do not want to resort to force unless they are compelled to do so.
The most plausible argument that has been advanced in favour of this disposition is the one made last night by the Minister of Justice. He explained that on account of certain judicial interpretations of our constitution, it would be doubtful if the government could exercise in matters of relief all the powers "contemplated in this legislation unless it were connected with the basic and broad principle that the government is primarily loaded with the responsibility of preserving peace, order and good government in Canada. That is what I had in mind when the resolution was before the house, and for that reason I did not mention that part of it; I waited for the bill. But if the object of the government^ is what was stated by the Minister of Justice last night, why would they not change the preamble of their bill and the clauses which derive from that preamble, in this way? I pass over the first part of the preamble and I come to the sixth line. AVhy not phrase it in this manner?
And whereas it is necessary for the maintenance of peace, order and good government in Canada that parliament should support and supplement the relief measures of the provinces and other bodies-
And so forth. That would make it quite clear as the basic principle of the law that the government are adopting relief measures and, so to speak, are going beyond the ordinary and normal boundaries of their jurisdiction in order to preserve peace, order and good government. That would mean that the first object of the government is to maintain peace, order and good government by giving relief to the sufferers. That would be serving notice to all the suffering classes that the first thing they will receive from the government, after parliament has given its authorization, is relief; and then such measures as may be necessary to preserve peace, such measures of force as may be required to maintain good order, would come not as a preliminary or as a separate subject from that of relief, while being connected in the same law, but would be exercised as a sanction to the preliminary measures taken by the government for the

Farm and Unemployment Relief
relief of the suffering classes. It is of advantage, it seems to me, as a means in the hands of the government of alleviating that feeling of distrust and disquietude which is arising much more quickly than the government realize since the introduction of this bill. Let us not make the mistake usually committed in parliament of thinking that, when we come to the last days of the session and after such discussions as those which have accompanied the Beauharnois affair, the people are concerned only with those things which have excited the nerves and feelings of parliament. No. The people at large are primarily concerned with what relates to their liberty and their material comfort. At the present time, there are in Canada millions of people who do not care a penny what parliament is going to do with Beauharnois, but who care very much what they themselves are going to get and give to their children next winter. There are also large numbers of people, especially in the big centres, who are very much disquieted at what the social order will be in those cities, when thousands and thousands of transient workers, men who have no relations with the community in which they live, who have no homes, who cannot be traced to any domicile from night to night, will be on the streets looking for food-and here I agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre-who will not care about law, or order, or the constitution or anything like that, but who, if they have nothing to eat, will simply break the doors or windows of the bakeries or butcher shops and serve themselves. Of course this action would be bad; but would any human being, whether he be a member of parliament or not, say that this is not a natural instinct of the human animal, if you like, who goes out for food? We shall have thousands of these next winter; and although I advocate the taking of measures for preventing such things, if necessary by force, I advocate first that you put on the side of parliament and government all the moral strength you can gather from all classes of the community by making it quite clear that you want to feed the people before you want to put them in gaol.

We want to give them
work before we put them in gaol.

Quite So. In that I concur entirely. For example, I am quite in sympathy with those subclauses mentioned in clause 3 which define the powers to be exercised by the government. I have marked them with three red lines which is my colour of approval. It is quite right that this legislation should be very much broader than that 22110-283
of last year. I am pleased to give that ample measure of liberty of action to the government in regard to relief measures. In that way the practical object would be attained and t'he principle would be saved; public opinion would remain in a much better state and would be much stronger behind the government than it is now. I need not say that the political result of this legislation does not concern me a bit.

I quite believe so. I also believe the leader of the opposition is sincere in the amendment he is making now. What is the use of trying to minimize the motives of each other in these matters? We may have differences of view as to the details of legislation like this, but after all, we are all Canadian citizens; we are all in touch with individuals who are suffering at the present time and we all want to do our best in order to help -them out. It is in that spirit I am asking the Prime Minister to modify the principle of this bill and those clauses which attach to that part of the preamble so as to make it quite clear that the object which was stated last night by the Minister of Justice as being the reason for introducing the bill, is properly stated in the phraseology of the preamble.

I quite agree with the general sentiments expressed by the hon. member for Labelle, but it seems to me he has placed upon the preamble to the bill a construction which it does not necessarily convey. The bill in the preamble recites practically what the hon. member for Labelle suggests. We are in a condition of national depression involving the necessity for relief measures of an extended character. We all know that when such distress prevails an effort is always made to stir up dissent and dissatisfaction and to promote civil tumult and strife. I agree with what my hon. friend has stated with regard to the city of Montreal. From one end to the other, in large sections of that community, propaganda is being carried on night and day of a most reprehensible character, and relief measures to a very great extent will be necessary in that

great city in view of the large influx of population which is taking place day by day, to which the hon. member for Labelle called attention in the other stages of this debate.
And at other times this session.

And at other times this session.
This preamble should be read fairly, and read fairly, I think, it does not convey the impression sought to be conveyed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre nor in a milder way the impression which was sought to be conveyed by the hon. member for Labelle. The preamble says:
Whereas by reason of the continuing worldwide economic depression there exists in many parts of Canada a serious state of unemployment and distress-
That is the basic fact upon which the whole bill rests. It proceeds:
-and whereas the partial failure of the wheat crop of western Canada has intensified the adverse economic conditions theretofore prevailing-
That deals with a specific economic condition prevailing in the three provinces of the west, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. It proceeds:
-and whereas it is in the national interest that parliament should support and supplement the relief measures of the provinces and other bodies in such ways as the governor in council may deem expedient, and for that purpose should vest in the governor in council the powers necessary.
and so forth. That part of the preamble accentuates that the conditions theretofore referred to are such as to demand national relief, to demand, in other words, legislative action on the part of this parliament and administrative action on the part of the government of Canada. The preamble proceeds to state that for the purposes of relieving unemployment, and so forth, there shall be vested in the governor in council the powers necessary to ensure the speedy and unhampered prosecution of all relief measures. That is the main object. This bill may be founded, as the hon. Minister of Justice has stated, and indeed it is founded upon the constitutional provision which places upon the parliament of Canada the supreme duty to maintain peace, order and good government, but recognizing that fact, as the hon. member for Labelle has done, does not necessitate that that should be the basis of the preamble to this present measure. The preamble says: - for that purpose should vest in the governor in council the powers necessary to insure the speedy and unhampered prosecution of all relief measures.
[Mi. Cahan.]
To that extent we are in accord, I think, but no one could sit down to consider the drafting of this bill for the prosecution of all necessary relief measures with the knowledge that every member of this parliament has, and with the wider and more accurate knowledge which the members of the government have without-

Mr. Chairman, I had almost closed my analysis of the preamble of this bill. I was discussing this latter clause: -and for that purpose should vest in the governor in council the powers necessary to insure the speedy and unhampered prosecution of all relief measures and the maintenance of peace, order and good government in Canada:-
I assure hon. gentlemen that there is no sinister motive in the sequence of these several clauses. I had something to do in a brief way with the drafting of this section, and my own view at the time was that we were facing a national crisis of unemployment and possible distress, that the first duty of the government was to provide for the relief of unemployment and of distress, and to support and supplement the relief measures of the provinces and other bodies in such a way as might be deemed expedient. Then the further question acrose in my mind that some provision should be made for the maintenance of peace and good government from the federal standpoint. I am not departing from the view that the whole basis of this statute is the preservation of peace, order and good government; but experience shows that in all times of distress and depression such as we are passing through to-day, opportunity is given to inflame public opinion, and especially to excite the minds of those who are suffering from that distress; and I believed when this bill was being drafted, as I still more firmly believe to-day, that it is the duty of this government under these exceptional circumstances to take such measures to protect those who are in distress, in poverty and in need from civil strife and tumult as a result of agitation. I know that the day we were considering the draft of this bill I read in the daily press of France-because it happens that at my home we receive the daily papers of France-the text of what purported to be a semi-official document stating that special efforts were being made by a certain element of society to stir up strife in Canada owing to the present commercial, industrial and agricultural depression, and that special measures were being taken throughout Canada for that purpose. No person who reads the pamphlets and leaflets which are being circulated

Farm and Unemployment Relief
throughout this country at the present time can fail to believe that special efforts are being put forth. Therefore as part of the relief of this national distress it seemed to me perfectly proper and convenient, and even necessary, that the federal government should be empowered to take special measures in that regard. Consequently the bill in the form in which it now is met with my approval, because in my mind-and I am sure in the minds of those associated with me in the government-there is no sinister or subtle meaning or intention in its terms, but those terms clearly disclose the purpose of the bill.
With regard to the other constitutional aspect which is suggested by the right hon. leader of the opposition, it is well understood in constitutional parliamentary practice that usually in voting money a limit is fixed to the amount that can be expended by the government during the fiscal year. But after all that is merely practice, it is not law. There are no constitutional and no legal limitations upon the authority of this parliament. Parliament now is here to decide, the pros and cons of the whole matter are before parliament, and all that the government asks is that parliament, in the exercise of its discretion and its authority, shall authorize the government from now to March 31st next to expend such sums as may be necessary under conditions which are not now known, which cannot now be fully appreciated or estimated, and which render it impossible to determine whether the amount of expenditure necessary shall be $10,000,000 or $100,000,000. It seemed to me-and I am sure it seemed to other members of the government from discussions I have indulged in with them-that in a time of national crisis such as this parliament might well vest in the government of the day during these few intervening months before March 31st of next year authority to expend such sums as may be deemed necessary. To fix a sum too small would hamper relief, because no one has protested more vigorously than h'on. gentlemen opposite against the appropriation of funds by governor general's warrants, and this is not a matter to which according to the ordinary and constitutional practice such warrants would apply. It is not an unforeseen expenditure such as would usually be covered by a governor general's warrant; it is foreseen, it is known now, and therefore parliament should deal with it. But although the amplitude of the crisis may be only dimly foreseen at the present time, I say there is no hon. gentleman in this house who has a sufficiently extensive knowledge of what will take place in this country within the next six or eight months to be able to determine with any degree of accuracy the amount of expenditure
which will be necessary in the interim. If the money is improperly expended, so much the worse for the government. It is true that here they are given a large and exceptional discretion in times unprecedented in Canada and therefore, to use the phrase of the right hon. Prime Minister, as the shareholders or directors of a company parliament must give a large discretion to the executive officers who, for the time (being, are to administer the finances of this country, whose duty it is in a national crisis to relieve unemployment, hunger and distress and who, when parliament meets again in February of next year, must take full responsibility for every act they have done or suffered to be done.
But I wish hon. gentlemen, so far as I am concerned, would rid their minds of any thought that in the drafting of this preamble or of this statute there was any subtle intent undisclosed in regard to dealing with the matter of peace, order and good government. In fact it was brought to my notice by some of the officials of our railways the other day that the men travelling by the score from one end of the country to the other, with hundreds being brought daily to the city of Montreal from the western and northern districts, were deliberately allowed by the railway companies to take passage on their trains, with no effort being made to keep them off because conditions were such that the officials were afraid that if these men were prevented from taking the ordinary baggage or freight cars as a means of transportation, the lives of passengers throughout this country would be endangered. I believe that to be a fair appreciation of the possibilities with which we must deal, and therefore, I think parliament may well authorize the government, in these exceptional circumstances and during these exceptional times, to take advantage of what may be called this exceptional vote in order that there may be wide-spread relief of the existing distress and that the ordinary peace and harmony which should prevail throughout the length and breadth of this land may be maintained during the coming months.

My hon. friend the Secretary of State has just said that with respect to parliamentary grants the principle of parliament limiting the amount that may be expended is a matter of constitutional practice rather than a matter of law.
Certainly.

And my hon.
friend says "certainly" in acknowledgment of that statement. I grant that he is correct, but if it comes to a choice, in matters pertain-

Farm, and Unemployment Relief
ing to government, between having regard to what is constitutional practice as against what at the moment may be the law, for my part, of tlhe two, I deem it infinitely more important to have regard to constitutional practice. After all it is parliament that makes the laws; constitutional practice determines how parliament proceeds in the making of laws and in determining their character. I say the first regard of members of parliament-what may be the first regard of lawyers may be another matter though I fail to see it would be so-should be the upholding, so far as it is possible so to do, of constitutional procedure and practice. I say that in this bill we are departing from constitutional procedure and practice as regards the manner in which grants of parliament are made and taxation controlled.
It is true that the Minister of Justice made reference to two or three cases in which he said the principle of parliament definitely limiting the amount of possible expenditure had not been carried out. I submit that the examples he mentioned only go to prove the strength of the principle and of the rule itself as it is laid down by all constitutional authorities and as it has been stated so frequently from this side of the house.
Let me deal with the cases mentioned by the Minister of Justice and, which were also referred to by the Prime Minister himself. The first was the Elections Act. My hon. friend the Minister of Justice drew attention to the fact that in this act in connection with what might be necessary for the purpose of conducting elections a definite amount had not been fixed.
Would imy right hon. friend pardon me-
Just a moment.
I have to leave the chamber; I have an engagement.

May I say
to my hon. friend that however much I may differ with him politically I shall never have any doubts as to his courtesy in everything.
I was speaking of the Elections Act. The reason in that case there is no limit fixed is that at the time of general elections, parliament is dissolved, the former parliament has passed away, and until a new parliament is elected no parliament can be called together to make a grant. Circumstances might arise in connection with an election where if the amount was not sufficient to carry out all essential factors, the election itself might not be completed satisfactorily. Therefore, in the realization that circumstances may arise when
fMr. Mackenzie King.]
parliament is dissolved which might prove embarrassing where an election is in progress, and that a new parliament cannot be called together until after the election is over, this latitude is allowed.
The next case referred to was the Expropriation Act. There again a certain latitude is allowed, but it is restricted to a definite specific purpose. In each of these cases there is a specific, defined object with respect to which parliament because of very special circumstances has allowed a little in the way of latitude. The act before us is not one that relates to a specific, definite thing; it is an act that is broad enough to enable the government to carry on practically the whole business of the country for six or eight months. That constitutes a very great difference. In connection with the Expropriation Act we all know it is impossible to foresee the sudden necessity which may occasion a wholly unforeseen necessity, and what it may involve. There is a reasonable latitude allowed, but it is always allowed in the light of the fact that the contingency cannot possibly be foreseen and that expropriation proceedings will have to be immediately confirmed by parliament and that in nature and extent they are definitely limited.
Another example given was sections 4 and 5 of the Finance Act, and in referring to those sections this morning the Prime Minister used the expression that it had been recognized as being important that in moments of emergency the government should have the right to spend certain sums of money without having first received authority, within definite bounds, from parliament so to do. I draw attention to the word "moments" used by the Prime Minister. This is not a moment of crisis; this is a condition of affairs extending over a year, a condition which has been continuous throughout the months of the past year and which is likely to continue for yet a year or more. In the case of the finance act, the act as I have said gives the power it does because parliament may not be in session at the moment of time at which the government must act in order to save a wholly unforeseen situation, A financial crisis may take place at any moment, and some act on the part of the administration may be necessary to save the day until parliament can be assembled. That is a very different thing from parliament itself, while actually in session, giving permission to the executive to spend indefinite amounts without limitation, not with regard to a momentary crisis but with regard to a situation which may last for months if not for years.

Farm and Unemployment Relief
The other case cited by the Minister of Justice was that of old age pensions. There, no definite amount it is said was fixed. In that regard the amount is very definitely fixed in an indirect if not a direct way, because the payment of any proportion of the old age pensions amounts is conditional upon the provinces in the first instance appropriating definite amounts of moneys for the administration of their old age pension laws and payments to be made by them on account of old age pensions. The representatives of the people in the provincial legislatures vote what is necessary for old age pensions, and it is only after they have so done and the money has been constitutionally provided that our agreement, which finds its basis in that constitutional obligation, comes into effect. The proportion agreed upon at present is 50-50; possibly on and after Monday it will be 75-25. Very definite amounts are fixed in the first instance by the provinces through their legislatures. All these seeming exceptions, studied in the light of their true significance, are found to be really such exceptions only as go to prove the rule, and exceptions which in the light of the contingent circumstances have due regard to strict constitutional practice.
There is one all important point which I think ought to be repeated. Hon. gentlemen opposite seek persistently to convey the impression that it is necessary to give these extraordinary' powers to the executive because it is going to be some months before parliament reassembles. The Prime Minister says that he is walling to change the date of the period for which the act shall continue to apply. He is willing to change it to the 1st of March. But again I say that if a condition is so serious that it requires unlimited powers with respect to expenditure, with respect to police and law and order, then when any such exceptional situation arises parliament ought to be called to deal with it. This House of Commons should not give to the ministry any excuse for not calling parliament under such circumstances. Once disturbances arise in this country and there is a general demand throughout Canada for the reassembling of parliament to deal with the situation, what we shall hear from my right hon. friend and his colleagues will be that parliament has already given the executive all the necessary powers-that they have unlimited borrowing powers, unlimited powers with regard to expenditure, the unlimited use of force in any way they may wish to apply it, and that they can handle the situation much more effectively than the people's representatives can by discussing the matter in the house. I say that we should not encourage any view of that kind; and to lend it even remote countenance is to help to create the very conditions in this country which the administration should of all be the most anxious to avoid.

In view of the unusual nature of this measure, and in view also of the importance of the subject matter, I may be pardoned even at this stage of the session if I say a few words on this question, particularly as very little has been said from this corner.
As to the measure itself and as to its extraordinary nature, I shall speak in a moment or two. But the first feature of the measure that strikes me forcibly is that it carries with it a confession of at least partial failure. A few days ago the corridors resounded with the acclamation of the Conservative party who were celebrating the anniversary of a great and momentous victory that took place a little over twelve months ago. That victory was due, in part at least, to the expectations held forth to the Canadian people that within measurable time the problem of unemployment would be solved. At the expiration of twelve months, after two sessions of parliament, a special session and this regular session, we find that not only is the problem itself unsolved but that it has reached such a point, involving so much human suffering, actual and potential, as to call on the part of the executive for such powers as are embodied in this act.
Again, Mr. Chairman, the measure involves another confession of partial failure. During these twelve months, and particularly during this session of parliament, we had looked for some definite policy of relief, some policy of public works, some detailed and defined policy which would indicate the method and extent of the public works involved, the amount and location of construction, and in a general way a fairly accurate concept of what would be done. But, again, we are met now with a measure somewhat vague but so comprehensive as to enable the executive to do anything along the lines of relief and to devise such means, to carry on such construction, as may appeal to their discretion but which at the moment is not in their minds. It is a matter of regret to me that during the last few months a Dominion-provincial conference has not been called to discuss this policy and settle upon something definite and detailed, so that we might know now the nature and extent of the public works

Farm and. Unemployment Relief
which might be constructed to provide employment in order to relieve the - present situation. I regret also that the government did not see fit to accept the resolution which I myself offered, and which was supported in this part of the house, for the establishment of a national council which would study these matters and the underlying problem from which unemployment itself arises, and from whose deliberations, if not in time for this emergency then for other emergencies, might evolve a policy so that no longer would the grim spectre of unemployment and suffering stalk this land. That, however, was not done, and it seems to me a matter for regret that we should find ourselves in our present situation.
. Now, coming to the measure itself, I must confess at once that to me it is an extraordinary measure, using that word in the proper sense. It is out of the ordinary, and in OTder to understand thoroughly how unusual it is we may define for a moment the functions and prerogatives of an executive. To my mind, as the word implies, the functions df the executive are to execute the express will of parliament as crystallized in the various law's placed on the statute books. But I cannot accept the suggestion that at the present time the government is usurping or seeking to usurp those prerogatives which have always 'been in the hands of .parliament itself. What the government is asking is that parliament should, of its own volition, invest the executive with those powers which properly belong to parliament, and to do so for a definite period for certain express purposes. My point is that parliament is asked to express its own will in the matter; theoretically ait least, parliament is at liberty to give or to withhold that consent and those powers. And if parliament does see fit to grant those powers it will foe the act of parliament itself by which this is done. Parliament for the moment will 'be over-riding its former wishes, expressed in normal times by way of statute.
I must confess again, Mr. Chairman, that under ordinary conditions, I should hesitate very much to give my support to such an unusual measure; for undoubtedly, under ithis measure, if and when passed, the government will exercise all those powers and functions which have been religiously retained by the legislative body. It will abolish, ait least during the months that w'ill intervene, that definite difference which has always existed between the legislative body and the executive body; and the executive body will for the time being assume the functions of the legislative body itself. That is the situation, and

it is undoubtedly a most serious one, and one that clan be tolerated only under most extraordinary conditions. Do such conditions exist? For some months, in common with other hon. members of this house, I have been giving consideration to the situation and to measures parliament might adopt during this session to alleviate conditions, to mitigate suffering and to rid the country of this grim spectre of want. I have come to the conclusion, reluctantly it is true, -that the only way to accomplish this purpose is to give to the executive the powers which it seeks. If there were other practical ways, I would be glad to adopt them; if it were possible for parliament to say at the moment what public works would be carried on, what program was to be advanced, how much money was to be expended, then I would not be ready to sign this blank cheque. The fact that neither the executive itself nor any hon. member of parliament has the slightest conception at this time of the amount of money which will be involved or the kind of action which will foe necessary, helps me in coming to this conclusion.
Or where.

Or where. I think there is an implied criticism of the executive for their not having held a Dominion-provincial conference so as to be prepared ,to leit us know what policy would 'be adopted and what public works would be constructed. But taking things as they are at the moment, I cannot see any other practical way of meeting the situation.
Does not the hon. gentleman think that there is another practical way of meeting the situation? *Could not a special session of parliament be called?
And lose a couple ol months.
Does not the hon. gentleman think that would be the proper way to proceed?

I have considered that during the last few months and, rightly or wrongly, I have come to the conclusion, first, that much suffering might take place before parliament could meet to deal with the question and, second, parliament being called at any given time, with a constantly progressive condition such as we have, there would be difficulty at that time in knowing just what would be needed in the immediate future.
There are two what might be called contradictory motives confronting us, and we

Farm and Unemployment Reliej
must adopt one or the other. We must stand by the constitution as it is written, retain within parliament those functions which properly belong to parliament and place the prerogatives of parliament before the necessity for action; or we may exercise this prerogative for the time being and for this purpose by giving to the government the power which it seeks. In either case parliament would be exercising its prerogative. As I said before, I have reluctantly reached the conclusion that with the conditions with which we are confronted, it is the wisest, the sanest and the most humane course to be followed, to give to the government the power necessary to deal with the circumstances which we find to-day or may find to-morrow.
When I spoke critically of the failure of the government to implement its expressed promises in regard to the solution of unemployment, when I spoke critically of the failure of the government to evolve and bring forward a policy of construction, be it understood that I was referring to industrial conditions and not to farm relief. That is something of which no government could have comprehension and to which no government could have given proper consideration.. It is a condition which has arisen out of a complete crop failure in a large part of this country. However, my criticism still stands in connection with the conditions which have been with us for twelve months and which are confronting us in increasing measure.
Where the question of peace, order and good government is concerned, I must confess that I am not a constitutional lawyer. In discussing this question some weeks ago with some friends I expressed the opinion that I thought we must give powers of general import. I expressed the opinion that in order to do so we must make reference to those general powers of peace, order and defence of the realm, or what might also come within the purview of a war measures act. These powers were not to be given for a wrongful use but rather that the government might have the necessary authority with which to carry out the relief purposes. I was glad to hear my opinion confirmed by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie).
Another question arises in my mind. Have I or have I not sufficient confidence in the present government to bestow these great powers? Although I have frequently quarrelled with the government over matters of policy, although I have offered criticism, I have that confidence in their integrity which warrants me in giving these powers, just as I would have given the same powers to the
late administration. I believe that every government we have had has been composed of men of moral integrity who would not abuse powers thus bestowed. I must suggest to the government what is undoubtedly in their mind, that in giving them these remarkable powers we are giving also the most unusual responsibilities, responsibilities which must be lived up to. Following the suggestions already made by other hon. members, following the pronouncement of the government itself and following some of the terms of this bill, I suggest that special attention be paid to a really constructive line of public works. There is throughout this country the need of works of construction which will add to the value and to the credit of this nation, works which will be of value and use to the people for years to come. I shall for one scrutinize very closely and critically the actions of this government. When we meet again I intend to make certain that the money, power to raise which we are now giving, has not been frittered away in useless or unnecessary pieces of construction. An effort should be made to keep away from doles, although I do not want to see any man or woman suffer from the need of direct relief. The work accomplished should be work worthwhile for this country.
I state my position without equivocation. I believe, perhaps reluctantly, that at the present time these powers should be given to the government in order to meet an unusual situation. I trust this government to use these powers fairly and wisely, knowing that they will be called to account when parliament again meets. I trust that in the immediate future they will make an honest and serious attempt to study this question and to evolve a .policy which will banish this spectre of unemployment and the necessity for action of this kind. I hope they will appoint some kind of consulting body and that in another year we will not be confronted with the necessity of giving carte blanche to a government to relieve the effects of depression, but that we will be met by a government which has fulfilled its pledges to remove the cause and solve the problem of unemployment for all time.

I have made one appeal
already to the Prime Minister to eliminate from this bill all reference to the maintenance of law and order. I have done so sincerely, and I believe the Prime Minister is sincere in his idea of incorporating it in the measure, but I consider his action is due to failure on the part of the government to realize the psychology of the labour men of

Farm and Unemployment Relief
this country and the effect this provision will have on that psychology. When one listened to the Secretary of State telling of the leaflets and other propaganda distributed throughout Canada and the effect that might have on our labour men, one could readily understand how sincere the members of the government might be. As I say, the action of the government is due to failure to understand the psychology of the labour men, because from my experience I believe there are no more sane, true, loyal citizens than are the labour men. We have had periods of depression before; we had for instance, the great catastrophe between 1914 and 1918, during which time the labour men of Canada were considered the bulwarks of the nation. I can recall then when the labour men had a grievance and when they came and assured the government that for the duration of the war there would be no industrial upheaval and no strike on our railroads. The newspapers at that time came out with big headlines saying what true patriots the labour men were. Now just because we have a period of depression, which was not caused by the present government nor by the late government, and because a few of our citizens are distributing leaflets, we have to bring down a measure of relief and incorporate in it a provision for the maintenance of law and order. I do not know whether the Prime Minister quite realizes the effect of this on the psychology of the men who will receive the relief.
I believe I know where the government is obtaining its information. To be fair I want to say this, that if I were on the government benches to-day, receiving the information that each one of them is receiving, and without having the experience that I have had, I might too be alarmed as to what is going to take place in this country. The majority of us know that the government have men situated in different parts of Canada giving them information as to what is going on in this regard. I recall the time when I used to sit in the Labour office reading these reports, and if one were to take them seriously, one might consider there was going to be a revolution overnight. I recall one time when negotiations were taking place in the mining areas of Nova Scotia in connection with a wage schedule, and if one were to have taken notice of the reports to members of the government, emanating from that quarter, one would have considered a revolution was going to take place overnight. I did not take those reports seriously. Knowing the mining men of Nova Scotia as I do, and knowing there is no body of miners in

any other part of the world more sane, sensible or loyal, no better citizens anywhere, I consigned that information to the waste basket. The consequence was that there was no revolution; an agreement was reached and it was carried out to the letter by the contending parties.
With reference to the statement made by the Secretary of State regarding men riding blind baggage cars and freight trains, one would imagine this was something alarming; that the railway officials were afraid of something extraordinary happening. I have railroaded ever since I came to this country in 1902 and I do not know a year since then in which we have not had hundreds of men, good loyal citizens, travelling east and west in this manner, their only reason for so doing being that they were not able to pay their fares. These men were welcomed in western Canada during the harvest time. People watched for them to drop off at the railway stations in order that they might assist in the development of the country in mining, harvesting and other projects of a national character. Therefore, there is no fear whatever with respect to the men who travel to and fro on the trains in this manner, and there is no novelty about it because it has been going on for many years.
It is quite evident from the remarks of members of the cabinet that they have changed their position with respect to this bill, especially as regards the provision for the maintenance of .law and order. The Prime Minister, who is the spokesman of the government, When he introduced this measure, made it quite plain what it was for. If hon. members will refer to page 4278 of Hansard of July 27, they will find that the Prime Minister is reported as having said this:
If the government is given reason to believe, as there may be some cause for its so believing, that there is a settled purpose in the minds of a considerable number of people-not large, numerically, but scattered over the _ various parts of Canada-to take action against the maintenance of law and order, or make attempts to impede the difficult task which we are charged, then we will take such action as in the judgment of the executive of this country, the cabinet who are the board of directors for the time being administering the affairs of this country, as will free this country from those who have proved themselves unworthy of our Canadian citizenship.
Those are his own words. Later the Minister of Justice changed the position of the government with respect to that, saying that it was only because of constitutional questions that this had to be based upon the principle of the maintenance of law and order before they could give these contributions for unemployment relief. The Minister of Trade and

Farm and Unemployment Relief
Commerce, when asking questions of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, showed that he had quite clearly in mind some disturbance was likely to occur, because he asked the hon. member what he would do providing some man out of a hundred would not g-o to work. The minister showed quite clearly that he had in mind that some drastic measure would have to be taken in order to compel that man to go to work or else suffer the penalty that is provided in this legislation. Surely the government must realize that is not the way to deal with one man out of a hundred who will not go to work when it is provided for him. To take care of that one man, or half a dozen men out of a hundred, we have laid before us one of the most autocratic measure that I have ever seen in any country, coupled with the provision for unemployment relief, As I said before, I do not want to take the position that the government is doing this with some ulterior motive. A government that promised the electorate it would cure unemployment, end unemployment, or perish in the attempt, realizes that this is not a good political move. I would say that on behalf of the government. This is not a popular measure to introduce. I do not say that the government has any ulterior motive. I think it is because they are unduly alarmed because there were a few stones or bricks thrown in one particular part of the country, and because of the information given to them by their agents, who may be unduly alarmed or who, as I prefer to believe, do not understand the psychology of the labour men of Canada, and who take one or two radical speeches to represent the position of the whole of the labour men of Canada. The labour men of Canada have been through trying times in many years, much more trying than at present. They have been tested, and I think it is wrong to sigmatize, as this bill does, the labour men in Canada generally and suggest that they cannot go through a depression and co-operate with the government without having a threat staring them in the face that if they do not do thus and so they are liable to three years' imprisonment. That is the reason I pleaded with the Prime Minister the other night to eliminate all semblance of threats from this bill. The labour men of Canada have shown very conclusively, even during this particular period of depression, that they do not need the threat of maintaining law and order to get them to cooperate, for during the last twelve or eighteen months I know of thousands of labour men in this country who are entitled, because of their seniority, to so many days work per month-no one could deprive them of it
because of their agreements and because of the seniority which they have attained after many years of faithful service-and yet they agreed among themselves to lay off so many days per month in order to give a certain amount of work to others who were less fortunate. With such evidence before me I do plead again with the Prime Minister not to insult the labour men of Canada by coupling in this bill the provisions for farm and unemployment relief with a provision for the maintenance of law and order.

I do not wish to delay
the proceedings of the house; in fact, I have said very little since I came here, but I must register my most emphatic protest against this bill. Virtually it suspends the constitution of this country, and establishes a dictatorship, and a dictatorship not of a political party but of the cabinet of this country. There is nothing that the cabinet cannot do under the powers conferred by this bill. Every right and privilege of citizenship will be abrogated by the passage of this bill. As has been claimed, and as was substantiated by the remarks quoted from the speech of the Prime Minister on July 29, when introducing the resolution, this provision is aimed at the working classes of this country. I .think the Minister of Trade and Commerce said to-day that it was aimed only at the bolsheviks, but who is going to define what a bolshevik is? The Minister of Trade and Commerce might include me in his definition of a bolshevik. Someone else might define him as a bolshevik. There you are; there is no one safe if this bill passes.

My hon. friend says that I said the bill was aimed at somebody. I interrupted an hon. member some hours ago and intimated that the bill was aimed at nobody, that it was for the purpose of providing aid to the unemployed. It is not aimed at anybody or at anybody's liberty, that of the workingman or anybody else.

The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre said that it was aimed at certain people and that certain people would be affected by it, and the Minister of Trade and Commerce said, I believe, and as I t.hink Hansard will show, that it was aimed at bolsheviks.
No. I made no such statement.

Certainly the Minister of Trade and Commerce used the word, and I am asking now who is going to define who is a bolshevik and who is not. What is the definition of a bolshevik? An hon. member suggests that it is one who is Opposed to constitutional government. If that is the defini-

tion, then as this bill does away with constitutional government, if only for a limited period, the government must be bolsheviks. If things are not better next spring than they are now, will this provision be extended, or are you going to go back to where you were before?
I believe that the amendment moved by the leader of the opposition is quite sound, although I would not accept the bill even with that amendment. I am opposed to the bill because it links up unemployment relief and distress with the maintenance of peace and order in this country. I believe the leader of the opposition is quite within the mark and very logical when he advocates the appropriation of a certain sum of money to deal with the situation. There are only five months to the first of the year, and ordinarily parliament assembles very shortly after the first of the year. Surely the situation in this country is not so bad at the present moment that this government .cannot estimate fairly closely what amount will be required for this purpose until parliament reassembles at the usual time. I noticed only yesterday in the press that the situation in Great Britain is considered very serious, and that financial difficulties may arise at any time. What did the Chancellor of the Exchequer say about it? Did he ask for powers to deal with the situation such as this government is asking? No. He said that they would call a special session of parliament if necessary, even before the 20th of October, to which date parliament had adjourned. I do not think there is any reason at this time for this government to ask for these powers. But suppose there is a reason. We in this corner have been, ever since the beginning of the session, drawing the attention of the government to the seriousness of the unemployment situation, and the government have steadily maintained that there was no unemployment situation. The Minister of Trade and Commerce, speaking on the 4th of June last, said that this was not the time to deal with the situation that might be anticipated next autumn. That is all very well for those whose stomachs are filled, and who do not know what hunger is, but it is very different for those who are unemployed.
As I said at the outset, I do not wish to prolong this debate. I think that nothing has been said so far that would convince me that this bill should pass. This bill is an outrage and should not pass this house. If the government had done their duty they could have got all the necessary information in regard to unemployment. The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Bpeakman) gave their dere-

fiction of duty in that regard as a reason for giving them this particular privilege which they are now asking. I do not think this house should grant it. At least I will take the responsibility of voting against the bill in its entirety, and I shall be glad to meet any member of the government before any labour audience in this country and justify my position.

Mr. Chairman, I
absolve the government from any sinister motive such as has been suggested with respect to the non-parliamentary control terms of this bill. They have no sinister motive that I know of; they have merely a fundamentally different attitude towards control of finance by the government from what we on this side have. And the same fundamental difference existed a hundred years ago, during the great struggle prior to the rebellion of 1837. Now my right hon. friend opposite claims to have put the capsheaf on our present constitutional status while he was in London recently, and yet he and his followers now want to revert to the colonial days, for by this bill they ask that the powers of parliament be abdicated in favour of the executive. That is just what the struggle was over in 1837. I do not differ with my hon. friends over there as individuals, I differ with them because of their Tory attitude of mind towards things parliamentary. It is a strange coincidence that we should have in this parliament the grandson of Mackenzie and the grandson of Papineau taking the same* attitude on this question as their grandfathers did on the question of parliamentary control of public expenditures. The grandfathers in this instance were sound and right.
They take the same attitude on every question.

If it is natural for my hon. friends opposite to revert occasionally to the Toryism of that day, it is just as natural that we should stand by the reformers of a hundred years ago. So we do not need to import- any personal feeling into this matter at all. There has always been a fundamental difference between the Liberals and the Tories on the right of parliamentary control of expenditures. That fundamental difference existed for centuries in Britain before 1837 and has continued in Canada more or less right up to the present _ day. A year ago I had the pleasure of visiting the West Indies and I was astonished to see what the colonial system really meant in operation. We had it in Canada prior to

Farm and Unemployment Relief
1837-the king's representative appointing the executive. In the West Indies they are perfectly haippy under that system; and there are reasons why they should be, but I need not enter into them now. But prior to the union of Upper and Lower Canada we had the struggle of the people for the right to control taxation and expenditure. I was raised on those conceptions. Whether I have been true to them all through my life or not -I hope I have-I intend to be true to them now. Everyone who has read about Lyon Mackenzie in Ontario and Papineau of Quebec are aware that in their struggle for responsible government they risked their lives, their homes, a price on their heads and everything that was most dear to them, because they wanted to secure what we are trying to preserve to-day, the control of parliament over expenditures, a control which quite unnecessarily is being abrogated by this bill. If there were some reason for taking so serious a step I would consent to it. It is not because I have not confidence in my hon. friends opposite as individuals that I appose such arbitrary powers, but because the Tory mind does not suit my mind. I do not know what my hon. friends apposite are going to do in their administration of the relief bill. From their conception of this matter at the last special session they are liable to do anything. I hope I have made myself plain.
Yes, you may sit down now.

Then I will leave that point. I would suggest to the Prime Minister that he ponder whether he is not putting himself in wrong with the people. This relief is going to cost us a lot more money than any sum that has yet been suggested. The biggest amount that I have heard suggested was $100,000,000. That sum will not cover the necessary expenditure for both -farm relief and unemployment. Does my right hon. friend want the cost to dawn on the people gradually? Why not say $150,000,000, which will be nearer the mark than any sum mentioned so far-that is, if we are to take care of both farm and unemployment -relief all over Canada. Is there any state reason why my hon. friends opposite should not foe candid and say: This is going to cost the country during itfoe next eight months $150,000,000? If so, I am willing to listen to such state reason, but I have not heard of any yet. There are two principles that divide us, and because of that I respect ithe views of my opponents, and I hope they respect our views and realize that in opposing the terms of this
measure we are not merely pernickety about something that does not amount to anything except possibly in theory.
We are proud to be the descendants of those reformers that I spoke of, and to hold to their conception of responsible government, and I suppose my hon. friendis -opposite are equally proud of being the descendants of the Tories of 1837 and to hold to their conception of it. But I would urge my right hon. friend not to divide us now on this question. We have got along together on many things, particularly with regard to our present status. Why make this rupture ait the present time by reverting to colonial status in this respect? I would rather have in this bill the sum of $150,000,000 mentioned, and trust the government to expend it properly, than depart from the principle that I have been endeavouring to enunciate and that was so much better enunciated by my right hon. leader. I leave -that suggestion with the ministry, and I hope their pride will not prevent them from modifying this -bill in the light of -the arguments that have been presented against the measure as drafted as a blank cheque, during the course of this debate.
