speechtext: Exactly, I say my friend the ex-Minister of Agriculture believes that.
Does not my right hon. friend believe it too?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am bound to say, as
I said this morning, if some of the communications that have recently been received are warrant for a conviction, you cannot tell what the amount will be. That is my difficulty, and has been for weeks. But I do put it to this house that confusion as to the grant and the expenditure of the grant is the difficulty that the right hon. gentleman opposite has been experiencing. The very statement that he read, the control of parliament over the grant, indicates that. That is the bedrock. The bedrock is not the question as to whether or not you fix the amount at $10 or $1,000; as if this great and glorious principle, which should be respected as far as may be possible, cannot be broken without smashing the constitution! To hear one of these hon. members talking about the constitution being destroyed, you would think he really meant it, instead of its being merely flapdoodle talk that he thinks will raise a cheer among the crowd. Go and tell men on the street corner, "Your constitution is broken,"

do you think they will believe it? What happens is referred to right here by Colonel Durell: the bedrock is the maintenance by parliament of its control over expenditures. It is going to have it. Did parliament break the constitution when it gave the governor in council power to guarantee the bonds, without limitation, of the Montreal harbour bridge, which reached a total of $19,000,000, when the original statement of the cost was only $6,000,000? Did that or did it not break the constitution? Was the constitution broken when the old age pension legislation was passed providing that there should be paid out' of the consolidated revenue fund any sum that might be necessary to meet half the expenditure, not of one or two provinces but of any number of provinces who might come under the scheme? That was done without knowing whether there would be one province or nine provinces affected, or whether the amount would reach $5,000,000 or $25,000,000. Was the constitution broken; was it destroyed; did it crack?
Then the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Heenan) and others spoke about peace, order and good government, and said that by this provision we were insulting the labouring men of this country. This provision is inserted to protect them from just such talk as that. There were two clear reasons for this bill. One was the constitutional point, which I always think it is difficult to explain when you are dealing with matters that have engaged our attention for the last half century, and when you begin to reconcile decisions from the Queen v. Russell to the last case decided a few years ago by the privy council as to the exact limit between the powers of the provinces on the one hand and the Dominion on the other. So I said last evening that I proposed to remove any doubt on that score with respect to section 2 by providing, through an appropriate amendment, that this relief, this provision of employment and this maintenance of peace, order and good government throughout Canada, should be as far as lay within the competence of parliament.
Attempts have been made to have it appear that what we have endeavoured to do is shock the constitutional susceptibilities of the provinces, but that is not so. One of two things had to happen. Either we had to undertake large obligations and responsibilities which, under the constitution, fell upon the provinces, and do it by declaring that it was done for the purpose of maintaining peace, order and good government, or we had to leave the provinces to do it themselves. Let there be no misunderstanding about that. The privy council has clearly decided that point, and this house expected us to take hold of

Farm and Unemployment Relief
this national emergency on behalf of all the people as distinct from the people of the provinces which might be affected. That is why we are trying to do it. That is why I say it became a national calamity when a hundred thousand people, by reason of the last crop failure mentioned last evening by the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Young) and the hon. member for Willow Bunch (Mr. Donnelly) suddenly became in need of food and clothing.
It may be said that we have trenched upon the constitutional obligations of the provinces to deal with these matters, and we had to do that on some ground. It was not the ground of war; it was not the ground of national defence or anything of that sort. It was the ground of peace, order and good government, that riots might not be possible, that unfed men might not congregate in corners to be inspired with the thought that their lot was such that they should prefer Russia to Canada. This was done so that our youth might not be banded together to decry the government of Canada, as has been advocated by the circulars which have been broadcast throughout the country. We desire to maintain peace, order and good government through employment, through activity, through food and clothing justly earned and work which involves wages. But there is the other side to it, the side of which every hon. gentleman has the right to think. Shall there be fraud in the administration of this relief? Shall it be possible that decent, honest, hard working men such as those referred to by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River shall be always subject to the insidious appeals made by non-Canadian agitators, who in some instances for the moment may have Canadian citizenship by reason of false declarations or flagrant disregard of the law which gave them a naturalization certificate? Shall these men be permitted to insinuate into the minds of Canadian men the cursed doctrines of the destruction of our civilization and the foundations of our government?
Those are the two issues, and this is the reason we have used this language in this measure. When it is said that we are trying to set aside the constitution, that is not so. Have we asked this parliament for a grant? We have. Is parliament to give that grant? Either this bill is defeated or we get a constitutional grant. True it is not limited, but it is granted. Why do not hon. members opposite vote against the bill? Why do they not summon up their forces and appeal to those on this side of the house to defeat the government? Once this parliament makes a grant that is the constitutional exercise of the powers of parliament; it
is the control of parliament, which is just the same as the control of parliament over any $100 item we have in respect to any part of the public service. It must be expended honestly; the auditor general must exercise control, for we do not provide that this money shall come from the proceeds of a loan which the government might put in a trust account and deal with. These payments are to be made from the consolidated revenue fund, and every dollar which goes through that fund under any circumstances is subject to the control of the auditor general.
That is what this measure means. If anyone suggests that because the government has not mentioned any specific fund they had in mind any object other than the safeguarding of two things, one the efficiency of the relief granted, and the other the guarding of the treasury of this country and the credit of Canada, he is suggesting what is not so. Those are things for which the responsibility rests for the moment upon the government. The hon. member for Red Deer made a happy observation when he asked if any hon. member in the house thought those of us who sit here to-day were seeking this measure for comfort or for pleasure. Does anyone think for a single moment that it makes it easier for any one of us because we have to ask parliament for a statute such as this? Then the cry is "Summon parliament." I can only say that this parliament will be summoned in due course, under whatever circumstances exist or may arise, but at the moment what is wanted is action and not words.
During all this session hon. members have been complaining that they could not get a statement, and they could not. During all that period there was not a day when at least one member of the cabinet was not thinking about this matter, securing information from every possible source, endeavouring to fit themselves to grapple with a problem as difficult as any that ever faced men in Canada. I wonder if hon. members realize that when war was in this country it gave employment at once in increasing numbers to the men left here, providing food, clothing and the other necessities of life. This condition which exists to-day is just the negation of that other condition. This matter is not being put through hurriedly and I should like to assure my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition that I have not for a single moment lost my sense of perspective. I only wish sometimes that my sense of perspective was not just what it is; my lot would be somewhat easier. I think I have just as clear an appreciation of the situation, from one end of this Dominion t)o the other, every

Farm and Unemployment Relief
part of which I have visited, as any hon. member in this house. From information which I have received and read and re-read and read again until I have 'been tired and weary with the reading of it, I know just what the conditions are. And what the hon. member from Willow Bunch and the hon. member from Weyburn have said is nothing new to me nor to the members of the government.
I say advisedly that in the early days of the session we had fervently hoped that with the spring, with the planting of the crop, there would come that betterment of conditions which would result, of course, from the prospects of a harvest, even although the price which it would bring would be small. We had hoped, relying upon statements made by men who had a better knowledge of world affairs than we have in the northern half of the continent, the great financial men to the south, and other great economists in other lands, that conditions would improve. The conditions that brought about the disappointment of our hopes in that regard are, as the hon. gentleman said yesterday, the act of God in one instance and those conditions in central Europe which are known to every hon. member of the house who reads. The condition in two countries, more than in any other, is responsible, together with the worldwide condition that results from the situation, to which I referred, arising out of the great war.
Those are the conditions, and I just ask my hon. friends this: What would you have done better than we are doing? We are doing our very best to deal with the problem, with a deep and ever-increasing sense of responsibility, which sometimes leaves men little opportunity for sleep and sometimes little thought, except the thought of what that responsibility is. But that does not in any way destroy our sense of perspective. And when this government asks the house for this legislation it does so for just the purpose mentioned-to preserve peace, which is the negation of war; to give happiness, which is the negation of sorrow; and to give order, which is the negation of riots and tumultuous assemblies in various parts of the country. And for the provision which will ensure these ends, of peace, order and good government, through constructive effort in public works and undertakings, giving assistance to the provinces and to the municipalities and other bodies, not depriving them of their constitutional functions but enabling them to collect their taxes, thereby receiving from the people the necessary assistance to carry on-

for this condition of affairs, I say, no men will be more grateful than these various authorities, that we have at least tried to see that they will not be charged with responsibility for those who are taking advantage- and I say that deliberately-of the very trying conditions of the present time, and of the great and difficult problem with which we have to deal, of those who try to incite men to actions which under normal conditions they would not think of.
With these problems, Mr. Chairman, we will deal to the best of our ability and after the most thoughtful consideration which we are able to give them. That consideration may not be the best the world offers, but it is the best we can give. We have asked parliament for these powers, not for selfish purposes, but for the benefit of this country. It is our bounden duty, by every means within our power, to establish successfully and to maintain in the present situation peace, order and good government, and we propose to do so by the measure which we have offered for adoption by this house. With the grant made, parliamentary control is complete, and it will be maintained by reason of the auditor general's control over the consolidated fund.

When I quoted this morning from Durell's Parliamentary Grants, which my right hon. friend will I am sure agree is the standard authority throughout the British Empire on this all-important subject, the right hon. gentleman asked me whether I would lend him the volume. He has, as opportunity has afforded, been carefully perusing its pages ever since. I have no doubt he took it away with him during recess-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No, I did not have time.

Well, he has been busy on it ever since. I have rather enjoyed watching him, because I knew what he was looking for. He was going through the volume to see whether, anywhere in its pages, he might discover something which would afford him some excuse for making of bis present stand an exception which might be justified1. I venture to say that if within the two covers of that book there could have been found anything that would lend shadow of countenance to what my right hon. friend is asking this house to do at the present time he would have found it, and we should have heard about it in a manner much more emphatic even than that which he has employed in speaking.
What does my right hon. friend say? He began and concluded his remarks by saying

Farm and Unemployment Relief
that control on the part of parliament was affected because forsootb the auditor general would have to do with the auditing of all accounts. Now surely my right ihon. friend has more regard for the intelligence of this body than to assume that its members are going to be confused as between what constitutes control and what constitutes auditing. The two are very different functions, and if hon. members will just ask themselves what the difference is they will see exactly where the difference lies between my right hon. friend and myself, and between hon. gentlemen opposite and those on this side of the house.
The quotation I gave this morning, which has been repeated by the right hon. gentleman, was that the bedrock of the constitution was control by parliament-not by any auditor general but by parliament-of all grants. Now that control is being parted with, because the measure fixes no amount.
Will my right hon. friend permit a question?

I should prefer to get through first; I will answer the hon. gentleman's question later. We are being asked to give a blank cheque; we are being asked to allow the ministry to spend whatever sums they like, to borrow whatever sums they like. Where is the control in that? The power of parliament passes over into the hands of the executive, and they are free to borrow as much as they please, to spend as much as they please, for months at a time, and parliament is not to be in session. Parliament has prorogued, the ministry will be absolutely free to do as they please. My right hon,. friend says the auditor general will go over the accounts, and that parliament appoints the auditor general.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
And the reports have
to come back to parliament.

And now my right hon. friend adds, the reports will have to come back to parliament. Well, I trust that before this bill passes the Prime Minister will insert an additional clause, which I shall move as an amendment, that reports be made to parliament of what is being done. Perhaps I had better stop to speak of that for a moment.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It is not necessary, if
that will please the right hon. gentleman.

I think it is
very necessary, especially where amounts certain to be spent are so large. When parliament was called to deal with the question of unemployment relief at a special session last
year, a definite amount was named in the bill respecting unemployment relief and was appropriated, namely, 320,000,000. It was deemed necessary then to insert a provision to the effect that reports should be made to parliament. I cannot understand, therefore, why in this particular bill, where no amount is fixed, and which confers infinitely greater powers upon the executive, no provision appears for a similar report to parliament. The act for the granting of aid for the relief of unemployment, passed by this parliament at the last session, contained the following provision:
A report shall be laid before parliament within fifteen days after the opening of the next session thereof, containing a full and correct statement of moneys expended under this act, and the purposes to which they have been applied.
That section has been dropped from this bill or rather has not been inserted in it and my right hon. friend tells us that he was told it was not necessary. Why was it necessary last year? It was pointed out by my right hon. friend that at least some semblance of the authority of parliament over what had been spent and the opportunity of review was essential, and if I am not mistaken that clause was included as a result of a suggestion from this side. A similar clause should be in this bill and before it is finally passed I propose to move an amendment to that effect. I do hope my right hon. friend will not seek to go the length of taking away even the obligation on the part of the ministry of reporting to parliament within a definite time after the expiration of the bill as to what has been done and spent under its provisions. That would be the last straw.
My right hon. friend quoted my remarks that the bed-rock of the constitution was that of the control of parliament, but he did not refer to another quotation which I made from the same authority. Mr. Durell points out that a corollary of the control of parliament is that there must be definite amounts fixed for the different purposes for which the ministry is asking parliament to make grants. Mr. Durell lays as much emphasis upon the restricting and defining of grants as he does upon the control of parliament in the broad sense. He says that one flows from the other, that one is the necessary corollary of the other and that you have not control by parliament unless you have your amounts definitely stated. My hon. friend did not quote that. When he ventures to quote Durell he should quote from the beginning to the end, and give to the committee the entirety of the meaning. I am standing

Farm arid Unemployment Relief
upon that authority and I am giving to the committee what Mr. Durell has said in this regard.
During the course of his remarks my right hon. friend seemed to intimate that as much as $150,000,000 might be required. Do hon. members realize that when the government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier was in office the total expenditure of Canada, including the interest on the public debt and the like, did not in any way exceed $125,000,000? Do they realize that when Sir Robert Borden became Prime Minister of this country during his early years of office the expenditures for all matters in connection with which this parliament voted appropriations did not exceed the figure which is being discussed at this moment as being necessary to meet this need? Do they realize that the amount which this government is asking us to permit them to spend without any limitation and, as my right hon. friend has just revealed to us, without the necessity of even reporting upon to parliament, is almost equivalent having regard to this period of time for which it is asked, to the annual amount appropriated by parliament for the administration of all the services of Canada, for the payment of the interest on the public debt and for the meeting of expenditures which have grown out of the war and the like? This amount is required for seven months only. When the proportions of this matter are thus revealed, one would be far removed from a sense of responsibility who did not realize what it may mean and what it may lead to.
My right hon. friend does not wish to call a special session of parliament. Let him then call the regular session a little earlier. We would be obliged if he would call it at the beginning of the new year or, better still, at the end of the present year. My right hon. friend will be fortunate if before this year is out he does not find it necessary to call a special session to save himself from the effects of what he is doing at this moment. He may find that he will need to call a special session to deal with conditions in this country which have got beyond his control owing above all else to the fact that he is asking this parliament to give him unlimited powers. Apart from the dangers which autocratic powers always seem to breed, having unlimited powers, the men and women of this country, believing that there is nothing under heaven my right hon. friend cannot do, may confront him with the things they demand of him to do and he may find it necessary to call this parliament to shield him in the administering of the enormous amounts which he is now asking us to

give in this way. There will be a period of seven months during which the provisions oi this bill will apply. My right hon. friend has said that this bill will expire on March 1.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: March 31 is provided for.
My right hon. friend said he would change it to March 1.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: If the opposition so desired.
We will certainly do all we can to reduce the time. Among other reasons I think it will be helping to save my right hon. friend from himself.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am so grateful.

The other evening my right hon. friend gave us the definite assurance that parliament would be called not later than the middle of February. That means that over half a year must elapse before parliament will be called. In the meantime the government will be free to do what it pleases, no matter what circumstances may arise. They are to have a bottomless well from which they may draw all the resources necessary to meet any situation. What does that mean? It means that parliament as parliament in making this grant is simply committing hari kari, we are turning over the whole business of this country to the executive to be run in a more absolute and dictatorial way than has been sought by any government from any parliament at any time since the days of Cromwell and the civil wars of that period.
Amendment (Mr. Mackenzie King) negatived.

Last night when the house
rose I was about to make a few remarks in regard to a letter I had received and read into the record. The Prime Minister and his colleague, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, seemed to be under the impression that I did this to embarrass the government. That is not the case. I do not see how any government could find anything in that letter to embarrass them. The letter was well and courteously written; it attached not a word of blame to the government for any of the conditions described in it. The writer stated distinctly he understood the difficulty with which the government is confronted.

And he addressed it to
the Prime Minister and not to the hon. member.

A copy was sent to me with a covering request asking me to bring it to the attention of the powers that be. If any government can find anything in that letter to embarrass them, I must say they are easily embarrassed. My purpose in reading the letter was to set as clearly as possible before the committee the exact situation as it exists. These people who have lost several successive crops, first exhausted their own resources, their own credits. Then they turned to the municipalities and the municipalities helped them out until their credit was exhausted. Last fall the municipalities found themselves in the position that they could not secure another dollar from the banks without the backing of the provincial government; their credit was exhausted. Now from what the Prime Minister tells us to-day, the credit of the province is likely to be unequal to the task of securing for the municipalities the necessary relief to hand out to these people. That is the situation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Surely the hon. gentleman realizes he is doing no service to any part of this country by making that observation. I did endeavour to disclose to the committee, without going into too much detail, that the strain might be such that money would have to be loaned to the western provinces. That is what I said. I have refrained purposely from getting into discussion of that kind which might furnish ammunition for those who attack the credit of the very 22110-284
province in which the hon. gentleman lives. If he desires to do so, I cannot help that; I have done my best.

I will accept the Prime
Minister's explanation. This is what I want to put before the committee: As the Prime Minister has said, the primary responsibility rests with the municipalities. The information contained in the letter which I read and in another communication which no doubt the government received, is to the effect that many people out there are in such straits that they need immediate relief. In this clause of the bill I find paragraph (a) as follows:
(a)	Provide for the construction, extension or improvement of public works, buildings, undertakings, railways, highways, subways, bridges and canals, harbours and wharves, and any other works and undertakings of any nature or kind whatsoever.
All that is excellent, but it will take time to plan those works. You cannot commence them to-morrow.
(b)	Assist in defraying the cost of the production, sale and distribution of the products of the field, farm, forest, sea, river and mine.
That is excellent also, but it will take time, It will not bring immediate relief.
(c)	Assist provinces, cities, towns, municipalities, and other bodies or associations, by loaning moneys thereto or guaranteeing repayment of moneys thereby, or in such other manner as may be deemed necessary or advisable.
I suppose that paragraph will cover the case of municipalities that are unable to assist themselves, but this will be subject to certain rules and regulations which will take time to work and plan out. My purpose in bringing this matter to the attention of the minister is to suggest to him-and I am not and have not been trying to embarrass him- that while these plans are being worked out, something might be done to yield immediate relief to those who are on their last bag of flour now and whose children are running around insufficiently clad, by letting the municipalities and the banks know that where it is necessary for a municipality to extend immediate relief in the form of the necessities of life, such as food, fuel and clothing, the credit of the government is behind that municipality in furnishing such relief. I make that suggestion seriously, and I hope the government will consider it favourably and not believe I am doing it for the purpose of embarrassing them.

Is it the intention of the government itself to proceed with any works under this provision or only in cooperation with the provinces?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Both.

What I have in mind is this: in the part of the country I have the honour to represent many public undertakings are required, the plans of which are already prepared, and the federal government could do a great deal of work without any cooperation on the part of the provinces or the municipalities. We have already, for instance, the plans of a bridge over the Rainy river. The United States government have passed an act permitting the Dominion government to build a bridge across there, but have refused to cooperate in paying a portion of the expense. Inasmuch as the bridge is for the purpose of, shall I say coaxing people from the United States into Canada, I think the government at this time could very well bear the whole cost of the undertaking.
The Minister of Public Works has in his office a report by one of the engineers in his department in regard to a retaining or protection wall along the south part of the lake of the Woods where the waters are washing away town property. There is also a public building that I think the present Minister of Railways and I promised the people of Emo because it was required and there are many other works of a like nature. I see the minister smile. This promise was made during election time.
I was not in Emo then. I was smiling at the facility with which my hon. friend makes promises.
I happened to meet my hon. friend in Emo in 1926. I do not remember what department he was minister of at that time, but I know he made the same promise to the people of Emo as I did.
My hon. friend's memory is of a very convenient type.
I am glad to know the government can initiate public works under this measure and we shall look for some of these undertakings to be carried out.

I should like to direct a question to the Prime Minister. Let us take that portion of Saskatchewan where at the present time there is such dire distress. In connection with the public undertakings mentioned in paragraph (a), is it the purpose of the government to permit the agriculturists

of that portion of the country to take advantage of the opportunity of rendering service on this construction work, or are we going to confine it to other classes?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Primarily, as I said before, that is a question for those in the province responsible for those matters. The language is that it is to enable the government to assist them in discharging their duties. It was not intended that the federal government should send somebody out there to employ eight or ten men to work at a given point. That is not a matter which constitutionally comes within our powers, but we shall not only try to enable but we will enable those whose duty it is to do that work.

Paragraph (a) refers to work which may be municipal or provincial in character. I have in mind works which are purely federal in character and which the government could carry on at this time, that would help to a considerable extent in relieving unemployment in the larger centres. At the beginning of the session I asked the Minister of Public Works whether it was the intention of the government to provide work of that nature whereby the artisans in the cities could find employment. I was unable to get any definite answer from the government. However, I see that the government are asking for an unlimited amount and paragraph (a) gives the government power to provide for the construction of public works, and so on. I would ask the Prime Minister whether, under that clause, the government will undertake to carry out federal works which will be wholly a federal charge and towards the construction of which the municipalities will not have to pay anything. It is hardly necessary to point out that many municipalities, particularly in the west, are not in a position to pay even the one-third that they were called upon to pay last winter. I think it would be much more desirable if the federal government itself would undertake such federal public works as are necessary and can be carried on in the immediate future.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I tried to make clear
to the hon. gentleman that the real reason we have to go so much further than heretofore is that because in a great many parts of Canada municipalities have been unable to collect any taxes whatever, and therefore they cannot carry on their undertakings. The provinces wherever possible have come to the assistance of the municipalities. To the extent to which it may be thought desirable,

Farm and Unemployment Relief
having regard to the circumstances of each case, such action will be taken as the interests of the country as a whole demand. That is the real reason why those words are there. Certainly it contemplates that there may be federal undertakings that will be carried on solely by federal authority. We expect that that will be so, but as I did explain to the leader of the opposition, the estimates provide for federal undertakings and public works that are within the contemplated revenues for the year. This extra effort on the part of the country will have to be one related to the communities wherein it is made, having regard to the conditions that obtain. I could not give an antecedent expression of opinion that might satisfy my hon. friend, but I told him that with respect to every province except one, and the premier of that province is writing a letter stating his position, we have already taken steps and obtained from them indications of the work they thought they could do which would be federal in its character, and undertakings which might be regarded as appropriate for joint effort. We have in addition, of course, the reports of our own engineers.

Let me give a concrete illustration of what I have in mind. In Winnipeg for a number of years we have been requiring a neiw post office and a new custom house. In times like these when there is so much unemployment I think that work of this kind should be undertaken. They are not works the expenditure on which would come out of the revenues of the country, but are capital expenditures. I am wondering whether under the provisions of this bill the government have in contemplation works of this nature.

There will be some
representations coming afterwards.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I say that they will all come afterwards-I hope my hon. friend did not misunderstand me. The letter has not been sent, and will nob be. sent, to anyone until after this measure becomes law.

It is postponing the
trouble.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I will admit that, but it is better to postpone it than to have it thrown upon one in the form in which it would have been had those communications been sent before. I think it only fair to state that to the house now, it being well along on Saturday afternoon. Otherwise it might well have been that the progress of the. measure would have been entirely impeded, instead of only partially, by the recital of claims of the various constituencies for consideration.
That is one of the most candid ministerial statements that I have heard.

The information just furnished iby the Prime Minister has forestalled much of the information I was going to ask for. I have no intention of putting forward the claims of my own particular district at this moment. Paragraph (a) provides for the construction of public works, and I take it that it is the intention of the government to proceed with such. I rather inferred from the remarks of the Prime Minister that he intended under this bill to supplement what should have been in the estimates for public works but was not. That is to his own advantage as Finance minister, for this reason: Any money that comes out of the loans for relief will, of course, be treated in a different category from the ordinary public works expenditures as provided for in the estimates, which have to come out of revenue, and if the Finance minister does necessary public works out of relief money he will be just that muich ahead in balancing his budget. This same section was in the act last year, and so
4478	COMMONS
Farm and Unemployment Relief
far as British Columbia was concerned notching, so far as I know, was done under it for the reason, I think, that the money was allocated to the provinces on a basis of each party paying so much. There was less reason for federal work last year in any case, because the public works estimates for the year had been ordinarily sufficient, but this year, owing to the need for economy, the public works estimates, as we all know, some of us to our cost, have been very severely cut down. I think this affords a very appropriate means of supplementing them. There is certain work which will have to be done, and to postpone it is in many cases a pure waste of money because it will cost much more to replace those works in a year or two than it would cost to do the work now. I think I gathered enough from the Prime Minister's remarks to reassure myself in that respect.
The other point on which I Should like a little more information is with reference to paragraph (e) which provides for assisting the provinces, cities, towns and municipalities, by loaning them moneys or guaranteeing repayment of moneys. In many cases we have got far beyond that point. Even if the Dominion or provinces were willing to lend money to the smaller municipalities, we cannot take it because the law forbids us to borrow more than a certain proportion, and we have already borrowed that proportion. Even if the government were to come in as a second mortgagee, it would only make our position worse. Paragraph (c) goes on to say "or in such other manner as may be deemed necessary or advisable." But that is somewhat vague. I notice that in last year's bill it said that they would make straight grants. They do not use the word "grants" in this bill. It says that the government may assist the provinces and municipalities "by loaning moneys thereto or guaranteeing repayment of moneys thereby." Also last year it was laid down in the regulations, if not in the act, that the cost would be allotted in certain proportions, 25 per cent by the province. 25 per cent by the Dominion, and 50 per cent by the municipality. We are not told anything about that in this bill. What I want is an assurance that despite the pajrtfcularity of this language, which would appear to confine it only to loaning moneys to municipalities or guaranteeing repayment of moneys thereby, there will still be just the same opportunity to assist the municipalities, and possibly the provinces, by grants to the extent they require, without requiring repayment.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
As I explained, I received a telegram the day after the bill was
[Mr. Neill.3
introduced on behalf of a large number of settlers in Saskatchewan who said that they did not wish to take money unless they gave a promise to repay it. So far as the federal government making direct grants to municipalities is concerned, I can only say to the hon. gentleman that the matter has not seriously engaged our attention; the relations between the provinces and the Dominion would be a very serious matter if they were directed along that line.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: But every representation that has been made will receive serious consideration.

The minister claims that we must not deal with the municipalities, we must deal with the provinces; but last year the dominion government, quite properly perhaps, imposed a stipulation that the municipality should put up fifty per cent, which was rather a harsh condition. In that way the Dominion was dealing directly with the municipality. Therefore, suppose a municipality went to the province and said, "We cannot pay this," the province might reply, "We cannot help you because the Dominion insisted that you should put up fifty per cent."
Has the Prime Minister considered the question of registration? I am prompted to ask owing to the fact that last winter hundreds of people flocked illegally into British Columbia.

What do you mean by
"illegally"?

Through the highways and
b3'ways.
That is not illegal.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The question of the
registration of all those who may be out of work, especially in the province of British Columbia, has been taken up with the local government. It has been regarded as being the duty of the provincial, the city and the the town authorities to secure that information.
I am beginning to be afraid that by keeping silent one's attitude towards this matter will be misconstrued.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is the idea.

Are you beginning to
worry?

I have not changed my mind towards this bill in any

Farm and Unemployment Relief
single particular. When it was introduced I said that the governor in council was usurping the powers of parliament, and I still think so. The business of the government is to carry out the behests of parliament-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Hear, hear.

-and this is a direct reversal of that particular power which the government are asking for at the present time. But there may be some doubt about the fixation of amounts where moneys are to be spent through the agency of the provinces, and I take it from what the Prime Minister has said that that method will be pursued. I can scarcely understand how any other method could be pursued, because to reach the municipalities the federal government must go through the provincial government. In such a case I can well understand it would be difficult to estimate the amounts required. But in subsection (a) the government are asking for authority to construct federal public buildings, railways, canals and highways. Highways of course, are still under the jurisdiction of the provincial governments, and I assume that if there is assistance for highway construction the work will be done through the medium of the provincial governments. But I think the government might very well have made some effort to present to parliament an estimate of the amount that they wish to spend by designating where buildings would be put up, and the type of buildings, and so with respect to canals or other public works that they are going to undertake. Surely some estimate could have been made of the cost of such federal works so that parliament could have granted a definite sum for the purpose. As I said before, the government are going to pass this bill by the sheer strength of their majority. I have no hesitancy in saying that so far as I am aware they will do their very best to spend money economically and spend as little of it as seems to be necessary. But on the other hand nothing has been said so far to convince me that the government is pursuing the proper policy in asking for a blank cheque, for this is nothing more than a request to be granted authority to borrow money and spend it where they like, directly in opposition to anything that we on this side of the house may say with respect to the matter. But let it be known that so far as we are concerned, we make our protest in the strongest kind of language against this usurpation of power on the part of the government.

I should like to make one suggestion to my right hon.
friend, which I hope he will receive in good part, and which I believe would be helpful in the administration of this act. I am sure that of the amounts paid out it will be desired that as much money as possible shall go to the persons who actually perform labour as a means of obtaining relief. I gather that many municipalities may not be in a position to make any proportionate arrangement such as was made last year. Might I suggest that the minister in charge of the administration of the act keep in mind the desirability if possible, of inserting in all contracts with municipalities or provinces, certainly in most of them, a clause which would oblige those communities or organizations which may be receiving any federal money for relief purposes to see that the whole, or nearly as much of the whole as possible is spent out only in payment to labour. Let me give but one illustration which will throw light on what I mean. I imagine the building of highways will be one feature of the work to be carried on. I suggest that before any municipality or province be entitled to receive federal moneys under this act it be obliged to incur all the costs of administration, of superintendence, of equipment, supplies, materials and the like in connection with the particular service being performed. This would be a real check on wastefulness and would ensure the money paid out under the provisions of this act going direct into the hands of those who do the actual work. I have given a little thought and study to this question of unemployment relief, and I know that the method that I have suggested has been adopted in other countries with most satisfactory results. This method of cooperation might well be carried to the point where farmers and others who have horses or vehicles or tools, and who reside in the community in which most of the construction is being carried on, might be asked to contribute towards the work by supplying what they could in this way, the dominion's contribution being limited to moneys going to pay for the actual labour perfomed.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
This affords me an opportunity to say what I should like to say now. My right hon. friend and I had a discussion the other evening about these matters, and I availed myself of the opportunity to secure from him a record of his own experience when he was administering considerable funds in connection with a rather serious condition that prevailed in Colorado. I am grateful to him for the information which he gave me, and which this afternoon he has mentioned without indicating his part in con-
4480	COMMONS
Farm and Unemployment Relief
nection with it. I think there should be in every constituency a local committee of citizens to see to it that no one suffers, for if the people themselves do not have some sympathetic consideration towards one another to warrant that action, it is hardly fair to expect that governments shall carry the whole of that particular kind of load.
Would the committee act in an advisory capacity?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That would be its own
business.

I want to draw the attention of my right hon. friend to one point in connection with subsection (c). As to subsection (a), which has to do with the construction of public works, I do not intend to elaborate on what I said in regard to a similar clause last year, that if the Minister of Public Works were making an appropriation of S2,000, ordinarily he would have to give the house full details. This, of course, is a direct departure from that rule, but I do not suppose any protest will have any effect. I want to refer particularly to clause (c), however, having to do with assistance to provinces, cities, towns, municipalities and other bodies. In many places in the dried out areas one of their greatest difficulties is that for two or three years they have not had crops and have consequently been unable to pay their taxes, which have accumulated on the property. In many cases the property is liable to pass out of the ownership of those who have built, broken, fenced and otherwise developed it and worked upon it. I was wondering what my right hon. friend had in mind with regard to assisting municipalities at least to postpone the payment of taxes so as to not have people in that position deprived of their homes because of their inability to pay.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No one knows better
than my hon. and learned friend that only the provinces can deal with moratoriums and with the question of relief from the payment of taxes. As to what action may be taken by municipalities where taxes have not been paid and where the property of taxpayers is imperilled, that cannot be antecedently stated with any degree of satisfaction. I can only assume that the provinces will put that point forward rather strongly. I know in some cases I have already suggested to the provinces that they should consider what action they are going to take to protect those who may lose their homes through non-payment of taxes.
[Mr. Bennett. 1

There is one question I
should like to ask the Prime Minister on this section. One of the very worst feature* of the situation, at least in western Canada, is in connection with the debts of many people, and particularly of farmers, some of which carry 10 per cent interest. Under this act has the Dominion government power to see that a rate of interest not in excess of say 5 per cent should be charged in any case? I wonder whether under section 2 the government would not have the power to take such action.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Macleod brought this matter to my attention some time ago. I told him I would look into it, since which time I have been able to do so although it may be that the opinion I express will be subject to revision. The Dominion parliament has exclusive jurisdiction over interest rates; the evidence of that will be found in the Interest Act. But where contracts have been made the province has supreme and exclusive control, and the jurisdiction of this parliament is gone. That is, we may legislate as to the maximum rate of interest, as we have done, but where a contract has been made the provincial authorities, and they only, may deal with the situation.

I should like to remind
the Prime Minister that although the federal government decided, under the Bank Act, what the limitation of interest should be, at the same time the government does not restrict people from charging more than is supposed to be the limit.
Under individual contracts.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is the difficulty about the contract.

Section agreed to.
On section 4

Orders and regulations.

I desire to move the following amendment:
That all the words after the word "as" in the second line be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"may be demed necessary or desirable for relief of distress, providing employment and within the competence of parliament in maintaining peace, order and good government throughout Canada."

I should like to suggest to the Prime Minister that when the regulations are being drafted under this bill he consider such cases as I am going to describe. The drought area extends considerably farther north than it did during the

Farm and Unemployment Relief
previous two years. There are a few men with a little reserve left in the bank or elsewhere who, unless they can get fodder, we will say, through the means which will be employed in the granting of relief, will be obliged to buy in small lots and pay regular freight rates. If it would bs possible for them to get carload rates, which will probably be the *way in which relief will be dispensed, it would mean a great deal to them. Will these men be able to do that, or will they be obliged to buy on their own, at less than carload rates and under the regular freight rate? I think that is worth considering in drafting the regulations.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I have no doubt that what my hon. friend says requires the closest consideration but primarily it must be a provincial matter. All I can say is that those who are charged with the responsibility under this act will cooperate to the fullest possible extent to ensure the best results possible.

Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 5-Enforcement of orders and regulations.

I have just one word in regard to this section. I can scarcely hope the government will change its wording, but it is a little rough on those who may be affected adversely by some error on the part of the administration. As I read it, the government have power to make any orders and regulations they please and to vary, extend or revoke those orders as they see fit. But if in the process of making, revoking or extending the orders they make mistakes there shall be no redress on the part of those who may suffer therefrom. Under this section the government is free to do what it likes; it can make as many mistakes as it pleases but there is no redress for those who may be adversely affected as a consequence.
What is the reason for that provision?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That is a usual provision in statutes of this kind; to leave it otherwise is an invitation to claim against the, crown under every possible circumstance. It has not been unusual for the crown to take cognizance of situations such as those mentioned by the right hon. gentleman. This gives no ground for legal action, while stiff leaving the subject the right to complain, and in the estimates from year to year usually there will be found some recognition of that fact. That is all that is meant.
I may as well make this further statement at once. It was suggested that the courts might be wiped out by regulations made under this statute. No such thought was in the mind of the government, and that was indicated by the amendment to the previous section. It must be remembered that the establishment of the courts is in the hands of the provincial legislatures, and no power here is conveyed to destroy or wipe out those courts or to establish new ones.

That statement had not reference to the establishment of courts but to the reference of questions to any authority. It was not the wiping out of any courts; it was only the utilizing of various authorities for the determination of offences under these regulations. My hon. friend the former Minister of the Interior asked why this provision was necessary, and I thought that was the question to which my right hon. friend was directing his answer. That is what we should like to know. Why is it necessary to provide for a reference of offences under these regulations for trial, not to judicial authorities but to some other officers or authorities as are mentioned here?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am afraid my hon. friend has not exercised his usual care in reading this section. The words are:
All orders and regulations of the governor in council shall have the force of law and shall be enforced in such manner and by such court officers and authorities as the governor in council may prescribe ....
These are the existing officers and authorities. This does not establish new ones. Such officers and authorities as the govemnor in council may prescribe are the existing officers and authorities. The word "authorities" is used because some of those who are responsible for the discharge of obligations and duties before the courts might not properly be called officers but authorities. It is the court officers and authorities such as may be prescribed. They are not a creation of this government except in the sense that the Supreme Court of Canada, the exchequer court and other federal courts-

Any other court that
parliament might establish.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes; but apart from that this does not establish a court. This could not in any sense be said to establish a court. These words are used in the usual sense.

It does not sound as if it were referable to judicial officers. My right hon. friend has referred to other statutes
4482	COMMONS
Farm and Unemployment Relief
of this kind. I took occasion to look at the War Measures Act, and there is no such provision there.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
This is not the War
Measures Act.

No, it is a good deal
broader. But on this point-the matter of regulations-the provisions of the War Measures Act ought to be sufficient. My right hon. friend suggests that "officers and authorities" means "judicial officers"; that is his interpretation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Not "judicial officers."
The provincial authorities establish courts and appoint the officers, and this authorizes "such court officers and authorities" to be named for the purpose of carrying the regulations into effect.
I submit not, though perhaps I am wrong. I thought that the court officers and authorities were those who might try the offences under the regulations.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No.

That seemed to be the
reading of the act.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Look at it and you will see it is not that.
I do not know what court officers and authorities are for if not for that purpose. I thought they were the ones to whom the offences might be referred.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: In his political zeal-
No political zeal.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: -I am sure my hon. friend wishes to be fair. All orders and regulations of the governor in council, the section declares, shall have the force of law and shall be enforced in such manner and by such court officers and authorities, and so on. That does not in any sense take away the jurisdiction of the courts. But a constable, a sheriff, a bailiff, or other authorized court officer, may be directed to do these things.
He does not enforce the regulations; that is my point.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The sheriff?
Yes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes; the whole theory
is that these are the officers who do enforce the regulations. Certainly the courts do not enforce them, but the officers of the law.
That is what I am getting at.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
And these men are the
officers of the courts. We do not create the courts.

I am perfectly satisfied to have the court carry out the execution. But we want to see that trials do not take place before court officers or other authorities other than those properly constituted for the purpose.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No such intention was
in the mind of anyone connected with the measure.

I do not
see any necessity for having in this bill any provision that a person suffering monetary loss by reason of a change in the regulations, with which he may not be kept informed, shall have recourse against the government. He has no recourse anyway, unless the government is willing to grant it. These regulations are bound to be changed. Undoubtedly this is a new venture in many respects, and regulations that would seem to be workable under ordinary conditions will be found to be not adapted to the circumstances that may arise. The regulations may be changed at any session of the governor in council. A man in perfect good faith enters into some business arrangement under a regulation, and he wakes up some morning to find that the regulation is changed; and the statute provides that he has no recourse, except by the ordinary method of bringing the matter to the attention of the government and obtaining redress through government channels or through reference to the exchequer court or some other body. I do not see any necessity for including in the statute an obnoxious reference of this kind.

Section agreed to.
On section 6-Fines and penalties.

I believe the penalties
mentioned are intended for those who deliberately set out to disturb the peace. As this section reads, however, these penalties might apply to anyone who did not carry out the regulations in regard to the administration of relief. Let me illustrate. Last year we passed a relief measure and voted so much money to be spent by the municipalities in cooperation with the provinces. Regulations were drawn up by the provinces. In a certain municipality the council looked over the regulations and said, "We cannot carry these out. If we do there might arise a situation in which we should be personally responsible for the expenditure." And they refused to

Farm and Unemployment Relief
act until they had positive assurance that this would not be the case. With a section like this in force, an arrogant official could throw a man into gaol. I do not think that is the intention of the government.

We have no idea
what orders and regulations are contemplated.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I would remind the
hon. gentleman that we are on section 6, fines and penalties.

That is what I am discussing. It seems to me that these penalties are extremely severe, and we have not been given much idea what the orders and regulations are. If this has reference merely to the orders and regulations with regard to the relief measures, these are very severe penalties.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
From the fact that a penalty seems severe, it does not necessarily follow that it will be the penalty exacted. The penalty is not to exceed a fine of $1,000 or imprisonment for a term of more than three years. I have in mind

well, I must not mention cases that have been considered in this house; I will forget the one I had in mind. I pointed out, however, that the federal power, in dealing with some of these bodies, must entrust the exercise of authority to those whom we name, and if -they play us false we want to be able to deal with -them summarily. Suppose there were embezzlement or fraud. There was brought to my attention the case of one charged with responsibility who had derived great benefit while those who should have received assistance were defrauded and deceived. I think there should be a power to deal with such persons promptly, effectively and severely.

I must protest against this clause. It provides that one justice of the peace, a man very often practically ignorant of law, may sentence a man to a fine of $1,000 and to imprisonment for three years. Let us suppose that there are two or three hundred men in a logging camp. A few simple rules are provided for the convenience of the men. One is that they must go to bed at a certain hour, there must be no talking after a certain time, they must not smoke in the bush during warm weather, and so on. In some camps the men are fined a small sum when they break the rules, or warning is given and then they are discharged if another infraction oocurs. The minister has hinted that it may be necessary to put men into a camp. Those men will be in charge of one man. The camp will probably be located in some remote place and there will have to be a justice of the peace on the
premises so to speak. That man will be nominated by the head of the camp and will be under his influence. A man may break one of the simple rules of the camp, or other rules may be made, say in connection -with seditious talk. A man may say, "This is a poor dump," or "I do not think much of the blank, blank government." This justice of the peace incited by his superior officer may take advantage of this section and give the man a very heavy sentence.

That -could not be done
under this section.
I am talking about section 6.

What the hon. member is saying has no real reference to section 6. This section reads:
The	governor	in	council	may	prescribe
penalties,-
A limitation is being placed upon the penalties which the governor in council may prescribe.

I will read the section. It
reads:
The	governor	in	council	may	prescribe
penalties that may be imposed for violation of the orders and regulations made under the authority of this act, but no such penalty shall exceed a fine of one thousand dollars or imprisonment for a term of more than three years or both fine and imprisonment, and they also prescribe whether such penalty shall be imposed upon summary conviction or upon indictment.
I think that covers the case. If it was to be by indictment only it would not matter so much. The minister says that it does not necessarily mean that a man will be fined a thousand dollars, but I know of justices of the peace who would look at that section and say, "By jove, I will have to fine this man one thousand dollars."

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The discretion is not
there. The governor in council will assume the -responsibility of fixing what the penalty shall be.

Is a new criminal code to
be created?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It is to prevent that
very thing; this is to be something which will last only during the lifetime of the bill. This is to cover offences which may be incidental to the administration of great sums of money.

The minister told the hon.
member for Shelbume-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) that the courts would be invoked.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Surely, but this is not
a criminal code.
4484	COMMONS
Farm and Unemployment Relief

The hon. member goes
astray in thinking that the penalties are fixed by this section. This is simply a limitation upon the powers of the governor in council to fix the penalty, and unless the governor in council goes crazy it is not going to fix a penalty of one thousand, dollars or three years in prison for a man going to bed at half-past ten o'clock when he should have gone at ten o'clock.
Power is given to do anything.

After the penalties are
fixed for particular offences then they may be enforced. In the distribution of large sums of money through various employees more extensive opportunity will be created for fraud than exists under ordinary circumstances. The governor in council should be allowed considerable discretion in fixing the penalties to be imposed for such frauds.

A man who embezzles
public money can be proceeded against under the criminal code.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
This does not take that
away, this is to provide merely for the special circumstances mentioned in the bill. The attorneys general, the criminal code and the machinery of the criminal law will be still there. I thought I made it clear some time ago that the fixing of these offences to be dealt with by regulation and the power of fixing the penalty were asked for in order to ensure some degree of, shall I say happiness among those who have to do with these matters rather than the opposite. Instead of making the burden greater we have endeavoured to make the administration simpler.

No prosecution could
be taken other than through the ordinary provincial authorities.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No.
By way of summary conviction.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That is the case in our
courts.

It seems to me
that a regulation of this kind could be used to intimidate the men. If this were merely to provide for the punishment of fraud by officials, I would not have any objection, but this would apply to men who are seeking relief or who are engaged on government works. Although the penalty in many cases may not be as severe as the maximum, that
rMr. Bennett.]
penalty could be used for purposes of intimidation. It seems to me that we are setting up a temporary criminal code. We are changing to the status of crimes what might be regarded as ordinary misdemeanors or infractions of certain regulations. I do not think an infraction of a regulation or an ordinary misdemeanor should be put in the same category as a crime, even although that crime will exist only until March 1, 1932. It is a serious thing thus to adopt a new criminal code, even if it is only a temporary adoption.

This
is one section of the bill which I think I can support. Evidently the government is willing to trust parliament to instruct them as to how far they can go with penalties. The other sections are unlimited but in this case the government is being restrained to one thousand dollars or three years in prison.

This act expires in March
1932: Supposing a man is sentenced under it to three year's imprisonment, would that imprisonment cease on March 1, 1932?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

Mr. Chairman, as I said
this morning when moving the second reading of these bills, the right of hon. members to discuss every detail of the measures was reserved. At this stage I cannot usefully add anything to what I have already said as to the principle of the two measures in question. One bill adopts the usual language in such cases in declaring that certain works and undertakings are for the general advantage of Canada, as far as what may be described as the canal part is concerned. The other bill deals with the internal management and control of the enterprise, and in order that no question may arise as to the grant of water
which it has obtained by lease from the province of Quebec being recognized by this parliament in view of what has transpired, provision is made for that matter in the measure.
My hon. friend and colleague the Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan) has given much time and attention to matters of this kind, and I have asked him to deal with certain phases of the measure. When my hon. friend the former Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) has expressed his views we shall be glad to endeavour to answer any questions which may be asked in order that not only the principle of the measure may be considered but that any questions which may arise out of their consideration may be answered and dealt with as we proceed.

Dear Mr. Cahan:

Nothing in this act contained shall be deemed to affect any right that may be vested in the province of Quebec over or in respect of the use of the waters of the river St. Lawrence for the development of hydro-electric power.
In due course I intend to move that amendment. In order that we may understand the exact position I may tell my hon. friend that in the same spirit I propose to suggest two other amendments to Bill No. 143. Section 2 of that bill now reads:
The Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company, Limited, its successors or assigns, is hereby granted the right to divert ....
Then it goes on to say how many cubic feet of water may be diverted. By some of those who have discussed the bill with me, including Mr. Geoffrion, that was taken as an assumption on the part of parliament that it alone could grant the right to divert water from lake St. Francis, and therefore I propose to amend that section by inserting the words:
. ... in so far as it may be within the competence of parliament. . . .
That will oome after the word "assigns," so that the section will read:
The Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company, Limited, its successors or assigns, in so far as it may be within the competence of parliament, is hereby granted ....

Then it was suggested to me that section 3 of the same bill should be changed. That section now reads:
No further or additional diversion of water of the river St. Lawrence shall be made by said company except with the express approval of parliament.
As members of the federal parliament, and as members of the federal government we have certain opinions as to what may be the rights of parliament in the premises, but by that section we do not wish to declare that the grant made by the legislature of the province of Quebec has no validity. That is a question to be determined by the courts and not by a committee of the house or by members of this house. Therefore I propose to insert, in lieu of the present section 3, the following:
